problem: Every organization eventually hits the same wall: more than a handful of computers, and nobody can agree on who is allowed to log into what. A five-person office can survive on local accounts and shared passwords scrawled on a sticky note. A five-hundred-person company cannot — HR needs to disable an account the moment someone is terminated, IT needs one place to reset a forgotten password, and auditors need a single source of truth for "who has access to what, and since when."

The domain is the answer enterprises settled on decades ago and still rely on today. It creates a single administrative boundary — one database of users, computers, and policies — so that identity, authentication, and authorization are centralized instead of scattered across hundreds of independent machines.

Why this matters at FundedNext scale A prop trading firm like FundedNext runs Client Experience tooling, trading infrastructure, and internal platforms across many machines and services. Without a domain, every new hire, every offboarding, and every permission change would be a manual, error-prone, per-machine task. The domain is what turns "update access for this person" into a single action instead of dozens.

Without a domain, three business risks compound quickly: security (former employees retaining access), compliance (no auditable trail of who could access what), and operational cost (IT spending hours on tasks a domain automates in seconds).
concept: A domain is a logical grouping of users, computers, and other objects that share a common directory database, security policies, and administrative boundary. In Microsoft's world, this is Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS); the equivalent concepts exist in Linux/FreeIPA and cloud directory services, but AD is the dominant enterprise implementation and the one this session focuses on.

The core idea in one sentence A domain answers the question "who is this, and what are they allowed to do?" for every user and machine inside its boundary, using one replicated database instead of thousands of local ones.
Security principals — user accounts, computer accounts, and group accounts, each with a unique Security Identifier (SID).
A shared namespace — a DNS name (e.g. corp.fundednext.local) that identifies the domain and is used for locating services within it.
A common security policy — password rules, account lockout thresholds, Kerberos ticket lifetimes — enforced consistently across every member.

A partition of the AD database — the domain naming context, replicated between domain controllers within that domain (as distinct from the forest-wide schema and configuration partitions covered in Session 58).
A domain is not the same thing as a forest (Session 58) or a tree. A forest can contain multiple domains;

a domain is the smallest administrative and security boundary within that forest — the level at which password policy, most group memberships, and most day-to-day account administration actually live.
deep: Domain Controllers and the database they share Every domain is served by one or more Domain Controllers (DCs) — servers that hold a writable (or, for RODCs, read-only) copy of that domain's partition of the AD database (NTDS.dit). Multiple DCs in the same domain use multi-master replication: any writable DC can accept a change, and that change propagates to the others.

Naming contexts — how the database is actually partitioned Partition Scope Contains Domain (Naming Context) Replicated only within the domain Users, computers, groups, OUs, GPO links — the objects covered in this session Configuration Replicated forest-wide Site topology, replication links, domain/forest structure Schema Replicated forest-wide Object class and attribute definitions Application (optional) Replicated to specified DCs only App-specific data, e.g. DNS zones stored in AD This is the key technical fact that separates "domain" from "forest": the domain naming context is the only partition that is not automatically replicated to every DC in the forest. A DC in a different domain within the same forest holds the schema and configuration, but not the user objects of a domain it is not a member of.

FSMO roles that live at the domain level Session 58 introduced forest-wide FSMO roles (Schema Master, Domain Naming Master). Three additional FSMO roles are per-domain, meaning every domain in a forest has its own holder:
RID Master — allocates blocks of Relative IDs to each DC so that SIDs generated for new objects in that domain never collide.
PDC Emulator — the authoritative time source for the domain, processes urgent password changes and account lockouts first, and handles legacy NT-style authentication compatibility.
Infrastructure Master — keeps cross-domain object references (e.g. a group in Domain A containing a user from Domain B) up to date when the referenced object changes.

Domain functional levels A domain functional level (e.g. Windows Server 2016, 2019, 2025) gates which features are available — for example, fine-grained password policies require at minimum the Windows Server 2008 domain functional level. Raising the functional level is one-directional: it drops support for older DC operating systems in exchange for newer features, and it is independent of the forest functional level, which must be equal to or lower than the lowest domain functional level in the forest.

Trust relationships between domains Within a single forest, every domain automatically trusts every other domain via transitive, bidirectional trusts built on the tree structure (parent-child and tree-root trusts), all ultimately relying on Kerberos referral tickets to let a user in one domain authenticate to a resource in another. Session 57 covered trusts in depth; the domain is the object that a trust is established between.
workflow: Walking through what actually happens end-to-end makes the abstraction concrete. Consider a new hire joining the CEx team and being given a laptop already joined to the corp domain.

Step 1 — Domain join The machine's admin runs a domain join (netdom join or the GUI equivalent), supplying domain admin credentials once. This creates a computer account object in AD, establishes a machine account password known only to the computer and the domain, and configures the machine to use the domain's DNS and trust its Kerberos realm.

Step 2 — Interactive logon The new hire types their domain username and password at the Windows logon screen. The workstation's Local Security Authority (LSA) does not check this locally — it contacts a Domain Controller (located via DNS SRV records, exactly the mechanism from Session 56) and requests a Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT), covered mechanically in Session 54.

Step 3 — Group Policy applies As part of logon, the workstation downloads and applies Group Policy Objects (GPOs) linked at the domain level (and any linked OU level) — this is how domain-wide password complexity rules, drive mappings, and desktop restrictions get enforced without touching each machine by hand. Group Policy is the subject of the very next session, Session 60.

Step 4 — Resource access When the user opens a mapped drive on a file server in the same domain, the workstation presents a service ticket obtained using the TGT from Step 2 — no password is retyped. If the resource lived in a different, trusted domain, the DC would issue a referral ticket that chains through the trust path to a DC in that domain.

The pattern to remember Everything in this workflow — join, logon, policy, access — routes through the same triad: DNS (to find a DC), Kerberos (to prove identity), and the domain database (to decide what's allowed).
Domains are the container that makes that triad meaningful.
enterprise: In a mature enterprise, the domain sits squarely in Layer 4 (Identity) of this knowledge map, but it is the layer everything above and below leans on. Physical hardware and the OS (Layers 1-2) run the domain controllers. Networking (Layer 3) — specifically DNS and TCP/IP — is what lets clients find those domain controllers at all. Enterprise services (Layer 5) like file servers and print servers are domain members that trust the domain for authentication rather than maintaining their own account databases.
Where domains typically live in a topology
Single-domain forests — most small-to-mid enterprises run exactly one domain in one forest;

Multi-domain forests — larger enterprises or those with regulatory/geographic separation requirements (e.g. a domain per country or per business unit) split into multiple domains under one forest root.
Resource vs. account domains — a legacy but still-seen pattern where one domain holds user accounts and a separate domain holds resources (servers, shares), connected by a trust.

A firm the size and shape of FundedNext would typically run a single domain unless regulatory segmentation (e.g. separating a regulated entity's identity store from a non-regulated one) forced a split — multi-domain designs add real operational overhead (extra DCs, trust management, cross-domain group nesting) that most organizations should avoid unless a specific requirement demands it.
dependencies: A domain cannot function without several layers below it already working correctly. Domains are built on top of, not instead of, these prerequisites:

Dependency Why the domain needs it DNS (Session 39, 56) Clients locate domain controllers via SRV records (_ldap._tcp, _kerberos._tcp); a broken DNS zone effectively takes the domain offline for clients Networking Stack / TCP-IP (Sessions LDAP, Kerberos, and replication all ride on IP connectivity between Dependency Why the domain needs it 25-30) clients, DCs, and other DCs NTP / Time Sync Kerberos tickets are time-stamped; clocks skewed more than the default 5-minute tolerance cause authentication to fail outright Forest (Session 58) The domain's schema and configuration partitions are inherited from the forest it belongs to; a domain cannot exist without a parent forest Server hardware/OS (Layers 1-2) Domain controllers are physical or virtual Windows Server instances; their uptime is the domain's uptime
dependents: Once a domain exists, a large stack of enterprise capability builds on top of it — much of it covered in upcoming sessions:
Group Policy (Session 60) — policy delivery is scoped and linked at the domain and OU level.
PKI and Certificates (Sessions 61-62) — Active Directory Certificate Services typically integrates tightly with domain identity for auto-enrollment.
Federation and SSO (Sessions 63-64) — ADFS and modern SSO providers federate out from an on- prem domain identity.
MFA and Identity Governance (Sessions 65-66) — layer additional verification and lifecycle policy on top of the domain account as the anchor identity.

File servers, print servers, application servers (Layer 5) — nearly every enterprise service authenticates and authorizes against domain accounts and domain groups rather than maintaining local user databases.
Security tooling (Layer 6) — SIEM correlation, EDR alerting, and incident response all key off the domain username as the identity anchor tying a human to an action.
security: The domain is simultaneously the most valuable and most attacked object in enterprise IT, because compromising it compromises everything that trusts it.
Domain Admins group — membership grants full control over every object in the domain; a compromised Domain Admin credential is a compromised domain.
Domain Controllers — physical or virtual access to a DC (or its NTDS.dit file and SYSTEM registry hive) can yield every password hash in the domain via a technique like DCSync or offline extraction.
Kerberos tickets — Golden Ticket and Silver Ticket attacks forge Kerberos tickets using stolen key material (the krbtgt account hash for Golden Tickets) to impersonate any user indefinitely.
Defensive practices anchored at the domain level

Tiered administration model — separating Tier 0 (DCs, domain admin credentials), Tier 1 (servers), and Tier 2 (workstations) so that a compromised workstation credential cannot reach domain admin rights.
Fine-grained password policies — stronger requirements for privileged accounts than for standard users, applied via Password Settings Objects (PSOs).
Regular krbtgt password rotation — limits the window a stolen krbtgt hash remains useful for Golden Ticket forgery.
Least privilege and group nesting discipline — avoiding broad, permanent membership in Domain Admins in favor of just-in-time elevation where possible.

The single fact worth memorizing Whoever controls the domain controllers controls the domain — and by extension, in most enterprises, effectively controls every domain-joined machine and every domain account. This is why DCs get the strictest physical, network, and patching controls of any server class in the environment.
troubleshooting: Domain issues tend to surface as authentication failures, so the debugging path almost always starts by isolating which of the three dependencies from Section 6 broke.

Symptom Likely Cause First Diagnostic Step "Trust relationship between this workstation and the domain failed" Machine account password out of sync with AD Rejoin the domain or reset the computer account (Test- ComputerSecureChannel - Repair) Users intermittently can't log on DC unreachable or DNS returning a bad/unavailable DC nslookup against the domain's SRV records; nltest /dsgetdc:<domain> "Clock skew too great" Kerberos errors Client or DC time drifted beyond ~5 minutes w32tm /query /status; verify PDC Emulator is a valid time source Group Policy not applying Replication delay, GPO link/scope issue, or DNS problem preventing SYSVOL access gpresult /h report.html; check SYSVOL replication status Replication errors between DCs Network partition, DNS misconfiguration, or USN rollback repadmin /replsummary;

repadmin /showrepl A useful mental checklist: name resolution first (can the client find a DC via DNS?), then time (is Kerberos within tolerance?), then connectivity (can the client actually reach the DC on the required ports?), then the object itself (is the account or computer object healthy — not locked, not expired, not disabled?).
example: A mid-size financial services firm with roughly 800 employees runs a single-domain, single-forest Active Directory environment: corp.example.com, backed by three domain controllers across two data centers for redundancy. New-hire onboarding creates the AD user object first — everything downstream (email mailbox provisioning, VPN access, file share permissions, internal application single sign-on) is triggered off that one domain account via group membership and provisioning scripts.

Compliance audits for such firms routinely start from the domain: auditors pull the Domain Admins membership list, review password policy settings enforced at the domain level, and check for stale computer or user accounts. This is a direct, practical illustration of Section 1's business problem — the domain is literally the artifact regulators point to when they ask "prove you know who has access to what."

When such firms plan expansion into a new regulatory jurisdiction, the recurring architectural debate is exactly the one described in Section 5: add a second domain for genuine regulatory segmentation, or keep a single domain and rely on OU structure and Group Policy scoping — the latter is usually preferred unless a regulator specifically mandates directory-level separation.
cloud: Cloud providers don't eliminate the domain concept — they extend or replace it with tenant-based directory services. Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is conceptually the cloud successor to the on- prem AD domain, but it is not simply "AD in the cloud": Entra ID uses a flat tenant model rather than the hierarchical domain/OU structure, authenticates primarily over HTTPS-based protocols (OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, SAML) rather than Kerberos, and has no direct equivalent of Group Policy (Intune/Endpoint Manager fills that role instead).

Hybrid identity — the pattern most enterprises actually run Most organizations don't fully replace their on-prem domain; they connect it to a cloud tenant using Entra Connect (Azure AD Connect), which synchronizes user and group objects from the on-prem domain into Entra ID, optionally with password hash sync or pass-through authentication. This lets a single domain account log into both on-prem file servers and cloud SaaS applications.
AWS equivalent: AWS Directory Service, which can run a genuine managed Microsoft AD domain or a simpler AD Connector that proxies to an existing on-prem domain.
Google Cloud equivalent: Google Cloud Directory Sync plus Cloud Identity, following a similar sync- from-on-prem pattern.

For a company evaluating cloud migration, the domain question becomes: keep the on-prem domain as the authoritative source and sync outward, or migrate identity authority entirely to the cloud tenant and retire on-prem domain controllers. Most large enterprises stay hybrid for years because legacy on-prem applications still expect Kerberos and LDAP, which cloud-native directories don't natively provide.
automation: Domain administration at scale is almost never done by hand through the GUI — it's scripted, both for speed and for the auditability that Section 1's business problem demands.

PowerShell — the primary tool # Create a new user in a specific OU New-ADUser -Name "Jerin Prova" - SamAccountName "jprova" ` -UserPrincipalName "jprova@corp.fundednext.local" ` -Path "OU=CEx,OU=Users,DC=corp,DC=fundednext,DC=local" ` -Enabled $true -AccountPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString "Temp Password") # Bulk-disable accounts that haven't logged in for 90+ days Search-ADAccount - AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00 -UsersOnly | Disable-ADAccount # Check replication health across all domain controllers repadmin /replsummary These same patterns — bulk operations, scheduled audits, provisioning triggered by an event — are exactly what Session 104 (PowerShell) and Session 110 (Configuration Management) will formalize as reusable automation. Domain administration is one of the clearest, highest-value early use cases for scripting in an enterprise IT career.

Infrastructure-as-Code angle Terraform and similar tools can manage AD objects (via providers) or, more commonly, manage the cloud-side directory (Entra ID app registrations, group assignments) declaratively, keeping identity configuration in version control rather than as untracked manual changes — directly mirroring the Git- based discipline already familiar from Aptimetric's development workflow.
career: Active Directory domain administration remains one of the most consistently in-demand enterprise IT skills, because the vast majority of mid-size and large organizations still run at least a hybrid AD environment, even as they adopt cloud identity in parallel.
Entry point: Help desk and Tier 1 support roles routinely involve AD user/computer administration — unlocking accounts, resetting passwords, moving objects between OUs.
Mid-level: Systems Administrator and Identity/Access Management roles own domain health, Group Policy design, and trust architecture.
Senior: Enterprise architects design multi-domain/multi-forest topologies, hybrid identity strategy (on-prem to cloud), and lead migrations like Windows Server end-of-life domain controller upgrades.
Certifications that validate this knowledge directly include Microsoft's identity-track certifications (e.g.
Identity and Access Administrator Associate) and, more broadly, the practical experience of having stood up and administered a lab domain — which is exactly what Section 19's lab below builds toward.
interview: Question Strong Answer What's the difference between a domain, a tree, and a forest?

A domain is the smallest administrative/security boundary with its own database partition and policy; a tree is a set of domains sharing a contiguous DNS namespace; a forest is the top-level security boundary containing one or more trees, sharing schema and configuration.
Why can a compromised workstation credential still lead to full domain compromise?

Because of credential caching and lateral movement — cached admin credentials, unconstrained delegation, or weak tiering can let an attacker pivot from a low-value workstation to Domain Admin if the tiered administration model isn't enforced.
What are the three domain-level FSMO roles and what does each do?
RID Master (allocates SID pools), PDC Emulator (time source, urgent password changes, legacy compatibility), and Infrastructure Master (keeps cross-domain object references current).
Why would an organization choose multiple domains over one domain with OUs?

Usually only for genuine regulatory or geopolitical separation requiring a distinct security boundary (different password policy, different admin group) — otherwise a single domain with OU structure is simpler and lower-overhead.
How does a Golden Ticket attack work, and what does it target?

It forges a Kerberos TGT using a stolen krbtgt account password hash, letting an attacker impersonate any user (including Domain Admin) without needing that user's actual password, until the krbtgt password is rotated.
misconceptions: "A domain and a forest are basically the same thing." They're not — a forest is the actual security boundary (distinct schema/configuration trust it, not domains); multiple domains inside one forest still share schema, configuration, and implicit trust with each other.

"Joining a domain just means the computer uses a shared login list." Domain join changes fundamental trust and authentication behavior — the machine gets its own account and secure channel to the domain, and Kerberos, not just password lookups, becomes the authentication mechanism for everything.

"More domains means better security segmentation." More domains mostly means more administrative overhead and more trust relationships to secure; genuine security segmentation usually comes from OUs, tiering, and Group Policy scoping within one well-run domain, not from multiplying domains.

"Cloud identity (Entra ID) is just AD hosted in the cloud." It's architecturally different — flat tenant instead of hierarchical domain/OU, web-protocol authentication instead of Kerberos — connected to on-prem AD via sync tools, not a lift-and-shift of the same technology.

"If the domain controller is up, the domain is healthy." A DC can be running while replication is broken, SYSVOL is out of sync, or time drift is silently breaking Kerberos for a subset of users — "up" and "healthy" are different checks.
anchors: Domain = the smallest security boundary with its own database partition, password policy, and admin group — think "the actual walls," where a forest is "the property line."
Three domain-only FSMO roles: RID (IDs), PDC Emulator (time + legacy + urgent changes), Infrastructure (cross-domain references) — remember as "IDs, Time, References."
Every domain login is DNS → Kerberos → Database: find the DC, prove who you are, look up what you're allowed to do.
Domain Admins group = keys to the kingdom; Tier 0 protection exists specifically because of this.
Entra ID is a cousin, not a clone — flat tenant, web protocols, synced from on-prem via Entra Connect in most real deployments.

lab: This lab builds directly on any prior lab from Sessions 51-58 that already stood up a domain controller; if that VM is still available, reuse it rather than rebuilding.
Objective Create a working single-domain environment, populate it with a realistic OU structure and a handful of users, and observe the authentication flow described in Section 4 first-hand.
1. In a lab VM (Windows Server, e.g. via a free trial or evaluation ISO), install the AD DS role and promote it to a new forest's first domain controller: corp.labtest.local.
2. Create an OU structure mirroring a real org: OU=CEx, OU=Trading, OU=IT, each under a top-level OU=Corp.
3. Create three test users in different OUs using Active Directory Users and Computers (or the PowerShell script from Section 12), giving each a distinct password policy expectation.
4. Join a second VM (a Windows client) to the domain; log on as one of the test users and confirm a TGT was issued: klist on the client after logon.

5. Deliberately break DNS resolution for the domain controller on the client (edit hosts file or DNS settings) and observe the exact "cannot locate domain controller" failure — connecting Section 9's troubleshooting table to a hands-on symptom.
6. Run repadmin /replsummary if a second DC is available, or dcdiag /v on the single DC, to see the health-check output referenced in Section 9.

Stretch goal Rotate the krbtgt account password twice (Microsoft recommends waiting ~10 hours between rotations in production due to ticket lifetime, but in a lab this can be done back-to-back) and confirm existing Kerberos tickets are invalidated — directly demonstrating the Golden Ticket mitigation from Section 8.

20. Personal Notes — Connecting to Aptimetric & the CEx Stack The domain concept has a clean, if inexact, analogy in the Aptimetric and CEx Agent Platform stacks — worth holding onto because it makes an abstract enterprise concept concrete against systems already built.

Supabase Auth + Row Level Security on Aptimetric is a lightweight, single-tenant version of what a domain does at enterprise scale: one authoritative table of identities (auth.users), with policy (RLS) deciding what each identity can touch — the same shape as a domain database plus its security policy, just without Kerberos or multi-server replication.

Aptimetric's proxy.ts route protection is conceptually similar to how Group Policy (next session) gets applied at logon — a central rule evaluated before access is granted, rather than each page independently deciding for itself.

The CEx AgentPlatform's admin email list and roster-driven access pattern is, at small scale, exactly the business problem in Section 1: a single source of truth for who's allowed to do what, instead of per-tool permission checks scattered across the codebase.

The tiered administration model (Section 8) — separating high-privilege actions from everyday ones — maps to a good habit worth carrying into Aptimetric's admin panel: the /admin/questions bulk- insert capability should stay gated behind a distinctly stronger check than ordinary user routes, the same way Domain Admin is walled off from standard domain accounts.

Net takeaway to carry forward: whether it's an Active Directory domain, a Supabase auth table, or a Google Sheet driving the CEx roster, the same underlying pattern keeps reappearing — one authoritative identity store, one policy layer evaluated centrally, and the more that stays centralized rather than duplicated per-tool, the fewer inconsistencies show up in access later.
